architecture: sparse n-gram embedding + direct linear softmax classifier
classes: A good query uses the rarest, most specific terms and drops filler words.
A sparse vector stores only its non-zero entries, which suits text with huge vocabularies.
A vector database stores embeddings and finds nearest neighbors quickly at scale.
Add the specific noun, the place or date, and remove words every document contains.
An embedding turns text into numbers so similar meanings sit close together.
BM25 scores term frequency with saturation and document length normalization.
Beginner ranking favors clear explanations, worked examples, and trusted educational sources.
Chunking splits documents into passages so search can return the exact relevant part.
Code search matches identifiers exactly and ranks definitions above usages.
Contradiction search pairs passages on the same claim with opposing statements.
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors; closer angles mean closer meaning.
Date search normalizes formats first, then matches the exact day, month, or year asked.
Difficulty ranking uses prerequisites, jargon density, and assumed prior knowledge.
Document search jumps to matching sections and shows context around each hit.
Duplicates waste ranks; deduplication keeps the strongest copy of near-identical results.
Exact phrase search requires the words together in order, usually marked with quotes.
Explainable results show matched terms and scores, so users see why each result ranked.
Facets filter results by category, date, or type while keeping counts visible.
For support, rank passages that answer the exact problem above general background.
Freshness boosts newer results when the topic changes quickly, like news or prices.
Hashing maps each term to a fixed bucket, giving compact vectors without a stored vocabulary.
Indexing precomputes searchable structures so queries answer in milliseconds.
Keyword search matches exact words; semantic search matches meaning even with different words.
Knowledge search works when articles use the words users actually type.
Legal ranking favors exact defined terms and the governing clause over mentions.
Metrics like precision at k measure how many top results were actually relevant.
Multilingual search indexes each language, detects query language, and ranks within it first.
N-grams are short word sequences; they help search match phrases, not only single words.
Notes search works best with dates, names, and decision keywords indexed together.
Passage search embeds each passage and returns the ones nearest the query.
Personalization reorders results using history and location, which can help or bias.
Query expansion adds related terms so relevant documents using other words still match.
Quote search matches the exact phrase first, then checks the earliest reliable source.
Ranking scores each result against the query and orders the best matches first.
Recall is how much relevant material was found; precision is how much found material is relevant.
Relevance ranking weighs term matches, phrase matches, freshness, and source quality.
Scores show how strong each match is, so weak results can be filtered or explained.
Similarity search embeds the text and returns documents with the closest vectors.
Snippets show the matching context so users can judge a result before opening it.
Stemming reduces words to a root form so running and runs can match.
Stop words like the and of carry little meaning, so search often ignores them.
Stronger evidence answers directly, cites specifics, and comes from reliable sources.
Synonym expansion lets a query match related words, widening recall without losing precision.
TF-IDF rewards words frequent in a document but rare across the collection.
The best passage shares the question's key terms and answers it directly, not just mentions it.
Top results optimize matching signals, not truth; verify claims against sources.
Typo tolerance uses edit distance to match near-spellings of query terms.
Zero results mean the query terms never co-occur; broaden terms or drop the rarest one.
